## Findings by module

### grid-down-food-5

- **confirmed** (ch-001.txt): USDA itself gives the boil safeguard: low-acid and tomato foods not canned by USDA-endorsed methods should be boiled in a saucepan 10 minutes below 1,000 ft plus 1 minute per extra 1,000 ft, and says this is not a guarantee and not a licence to eat food known to be underprocessed. Matches the course l3 wording and callout; the course cites CDC, the USDA guide is the primary source.
- **confirmed** (ch-001.txt): Sterilised jars stay free of spoilage if sealed and stored below 95 F (35 C); 50 to 70 F keeps quality best. Course storage rule matches.
- **confirmed** (ch-002.txt): Do not taste food from an unsealed jar or one showing spoilage. Matches the course never-taste rule.
- **refined** (ch-001.txt): Low-acid (pH above 4.6) per USDA: red meats, seafood, poultry, milk and all fresh vegetables except most tomatoes; mixtures of low-acid and acid foods are usually low-acid unless the recipe adds enough lemon juice, citric acid or vinegar. Tomatoes and figs can sit slightly above 4.6, so must be acidified to can them in boiling water. Course lists figs and some tomatoes; add milk and the mixtures point.
- **refined** (ch-002.txt): Course says throw out suspect jars but not how. USDA: treat any suspect low-acid jar (including tomatoes) as containing botulinum toxin, since spoilage may show little sign. Still-sealed jars or swollen cans go in a heavy bin bag in the rubbish; unsealed, open or leaking ones are detoxified first by boiling, fully covered, for 30 minutes, wearing gloves. Toxin can be fatal by skin contact too; clean surfaces with 1 part unscented bleach (5 to 6 percent) to 5 parts water, leave 30 minutes, wipe, repeat, rinse, wash.
- **extended** (ch-001.txt): USDA lists when properly canned low-acid food may be eaten without boiling: processed in a pressure canner, accurate gauge, current researched times and pressures for jar size, pack style and food, altitude-correct time, lid firmly sealed and concave, nothing leaked, no spurting on opening, no off odours. A usable checklist for judging a jar you canned yourself.
- **extended** (ch-001.txt): Why boiling water is not enough: C. botulinum spores survive boiling; low-acid foods need 240 to 250 F (about 116 to 121 C), reached in a pressure canner at 10 to 15 PSI, for 20 to 100 minutes; the same safety in a boiling-water canner would take 7 to 11 hours. Spores grow and make toxin within 3 to 4 days in moist low-acid food at 40 to 120 F with under 2 percent oxygen. Gives the mechanism behind the pressure-canning rule.
- **extended** (ch-001.txt): Nutrient losses: canning heat destroys a third to a half of vitamins A and C, thiamin and riboflavin, then 5 to 20 percent more each year in storage; produce can lose half of some vitamins within 1 to 2 weeks even refrigerated. Supports canning only a year's supply.
- **extended** (ch-002.txt): Methods the 2015 guide does not recommend: open-kettle canning; processing jars in ordinary ovens, microwaves or dishwashers; steam canners (times then still being researched); canning powders, which are useless as preservatives; pressure saucepans; mayonnaise-type jars in pressure canners; wire-bail and zinc caps. Extends the course's do-not list beyond the electric multi-cooker. Check current NCHFP guidance before saying anything about steam canners now.
- **extended** (ch-002.txt): Pressure canner safety: air trapped in the canner lowers the temperature and under-processes, so every canner is vented 10 minutes before pressurising; dial gauges are checked for accuracy every year and replaced if more than 2 lb out; if pressure drops below the target at any time, return to pressure and restart the whole process time. 10.5 lb at sea level gives 240 F; weighted gauges above 1,000 ft run at 15 instead of 10 lb.
- **extended** (ch-002.txt): Checking a stored jar before use: lid concave and tight; no streaks of dried food from the top; no rising bubbles or unnatural colour; on opening, no spurting, off smell or cotton-like mould. Store without screw bands so lifted lids show. Seal test after 12 to 24 hours: press centre (no spring), tap with a spoon (ringing, not dull), lid concave. Unsealed jars: reprocess within 24 hours, freeze, or refrigerate and eat within several days.
- **extended** (ch-002.txt): Pickles and ferments: acidity is a safety control, so never change vinegar, food or water proportions or use vinegar of unknown acidity (use 5 percent); salt in sauerkraut and brined pickles is vital to safety, so never cut it. Store jars away from heat, damp and direct sun; accidental freezing does not spoil sealed jars.
- **extended** (ch-003.txt): Mould on jams and jellies is not harmless to scrape off: mycotoxins have been found in jars with surface mould, and paraffin or wax seals are no longer recommended for any sweet spread. Sugar cannot be cut in traditional recipes without risking yeasts and moulds. Adds to the spoilage-signs lesson.
- **extended** (ch-003.txt): Botulism control by preserving method (USDA glossary): heat processing destroys it in canned food, freezer temperatures inhibit its growth, low moisture controls it in dried food, and high oxygen controls it in fresh food. A one-line map tying freezing, drying and canning together.
- **extended** (ch-004.txt to ch-010.txt (caution scan)): Safety cautions in the recipe guides: never thicken home-canned soups or chilli (no pasta, rice, flour, cream or milk; add at serving); never mash or puree pumpkin, squash or potatoes before canning; do not alter vegetable-to-acid proportions in salsas or use homemade vinegar or vinegar under 5 percent; lemon juice may replace vinegar but not the reverse; do not can tomatoes from dead or frost-killed vines; bleed and gut fish within 2 hours of catching; ferment only in food-grade containers, never bin bags; discard pickles that turn soft, slimy or smell bad. Each supports the course rule to follow tested recipes exactly.
- **note** (ch-002.txt): Quality and storage: can vegetables within 6 to 12 hours of harvest; can fish within 2 days, iced and gutted; never can meat from sick animals; lids seal reliably for about 5 years from manufacture, so buy only a year's lids; remove screw bands for storage; can no more than you will use in a year. Jars cool undisturbed 12 to 24 hours; do not force-cool a pressure canner.
- **note** (ch-003.txt): Do not home-can pureed vegetables, red meats or poultry (no tested times); can them standard style and puree at serving, bringing to the boil and simmering 10 minutes. Salt is not needed for safety in canned tomatoes, vegetables or meats (only in ferments). Refrigerator spreads made with gelatin keep 1 month in the fridge. Relevant if baby food is part of a grid-down store.

### grid-down-food-4

- **note** (ch-002.txt): Grid-down implication (our inference from USDA steps): a pressure-canner load takes roughly an hour or more of steady heat plus 20 to 60 minutes cooling, and a loss of pressure or boil means restarting the timing, so canning during an outage needs a steady, controllable heat source and enough fuel; an unreliable stove makes canning unsafe rather than just slow.

### grid-down-food-2

- **extended** (ch-003.txt): Microorganisms in a suitable environment can divide every 10 to 30 minutes, so populations become high very quickly. Explains why the power-cut clock counts in hours.
